The Sierpinski Triangle

Consider the following experiment: Place three points A,BA, BA,B and CCC uniformly on the border of a circle. Then we put one point X1X_1X1​ in the middle of the circle. From there we continously sample points X2,X3,…X_2,X_3, \dotsX2​,X3​,… by choosing one point Y∈{A,B,C}Y \in \{ A,B,C\}Y∈{A,B,C} randomly, and setting

Xn+1=(Xn+Y)/2X_{n+1} = (X_n+Y)/2Xn+1​=(Xn​+Y)/2

ie. a new point is exactly in the middle of the previous point and a random corner A,B,CA,B,CA,B,C (you will see in a second why we speak of corners). Lets do that up to 2152^{15}215. Then we get the following picture:

We see that a Sierpinski triangle emerges where the corners align exactly with our points A,BA,BA,B and CCC.

Suggestion: Try to lower the number of points to see that the points are really just chosen randomly. For a smaller exponent, the border will not be as clearly visible.

Lets think a moment why that happens: If we look closely, we can see our starting point X1X_1X1​ in the middle, exactly in the center of the big white triangle. We will call it a layer-111-triangle. The next point X2X_2X2​ will lie exactly in the middle of X1X_1X1​ and a corner. If we look closely again, we can find it in one of the three triangles, that are just a bit smaller. We will call them layer-222-triangles. At this point it is a sensible assumption that in general XnX_nXn​ will lie in the center of a layer-nnn-triangle.

Given this, it makes sense, that the points appear to lie on the lines in the Sierpinski triangle. The larger nnn becomes, the closer does the center of a layer-nnn-triangle approach a line. Since we draw a large number of points, most of them will be drawn so closely to a line in the Sierpinski triangle, that it appears as if we placed all of them randomly there.

We can even proof our assumption: Clearly, the centers of the layer-nnn-triangles are exactly the points that can be reached by choosing directions d1,d2,…,dn−1∈{A,B,C}d_1,d_2,\dots,d_{n-1} \in \{A,B,C\}d1​,d2​,…,dn−1​∈{A,B,C}, and then walking the steps d12,d24,d38,…,dn−12n\frac{d_1}{2},\frac{d_2}{4},\frac{d_3}{8},\dots,\frac{d_{n-1}}{2^n}2d1​​,4d2​​,8d3​​,…,2ndn−1​​, so that we end up at the point

∑i=1n−1di2i+1\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \frac{d_i}{2^{i+1}}i=1∑n−1​2i+1di​​

On the other hand, to sample our points, we also choose corners c1,c2,…,cn−1∈{A,B,C}c_1,c_2,\dots,c_{n-1} \in \{A,B,C\}c1​,c2​,…,cn−1​∈{A,B,C} and compute

Xn=((((… )/2+cn−3)/2+cn−2)/2+cn−1)/2X_n = ((((\dots)/2+ c_{n-3})/2+c_{n-2})/2+c_{n-1})/2 Xn​=((((…)/2+cn−3​)/2+cn−2​)/2+cn−1​)/2

Suggestion: To finish the proof, think about how a sequence d1,d2,…d_1, d_2, \dotsd1​,d2​,… can be chosen for a given sequence c1,c2,…c_1, c_2, \dotsc1​,c2​,…, such that the resulting points are equal.

Trying something else

Whats happens if we change parameters in our experiment? For example the number of corners? If we set it to two, we just end up with a line, so nothing interesting there. But we can make it more interesting by taking a point closer to the corner. For example, we could instead take the point

Xn=wXn−1+(1−w)Y X_n = w X_{n-1} + (1-w) YXn​=wXn−1​+(1−w)Y

for some parameter w∈[0,1]w \in [0,1]w∈[0,1] that we will call weight. Notice that for w=13w=\frac 1 3w=31​ we end up with something that looks like the Cantor set:

Can you find an explanation of why this happens? It could be similar to our explanation for the Sierpinski triangle.

We found two other well-known fractals that can appear in this experiment. Taking 444 corners and a weight of 13\frac 1 331​ give the Sierpinski carpet:

Taking 666 corners and again a weight of 13\frac 1 331​ give an assemblance of multiple Koch snowflakes:
